draft.title: The body's defences
card: The body has barriers that stop most pathogens getting in. Skin covers the outside. Mucus in the nose and airways traps germs. Stomach acid kills many that are swallowed.
If a pathogen gets past the barriers, white blood cells attack it. Some white blood cells surround and destroy pathogens.
Some white blood cells make antibodies. An antibody is a protein that fits one kind of pathogen and helps the body destroy it.
The body can keep a record of the antibodies it made. The next time the same pathogen gets in, the body recognises it and responds faster.
draft.remember: Barriers keep pathogens out. White blood cells and antibodies attack those that get in.

a.q: Which of these is a barrier that stops pathogens getting into the body?
opts: White blood cells in the blood
a.why: Mucus traps pathogens before they enter the body. Antibodies and white blood cells work inside the body, after a pathogen has got past the barriers.
a.clue: A barrier works before a pathogen gets inside.

b.q: Sam catches a cold virus. Months later the same virus gets into his body again, and he recovers faster. What best explains this?
opts: His body recognised it from antibodies made before
His skin stopped the virus from getting in again
His stomach acid killed the virus before it spread
His white blood cells ate it without any antibodies
b.why: The body kept a record of the antibodies it made the first time, so it recognised the virus and responded faster. Skin is a barrier, but the virus got in, so the barriers did not stop it.
b.clue: The virus got in both times, so think about what the body did once it was inside.

b.best: His body recognised it from antibodies made before
